summary: Specifies IPv4 compatibility mechanisms that IPv6 hosts and routers can implement, helping the two protocols coexist during the move to IPv6. It was replaced by RFC 2893.

eli5.summary: A bridge between old and new roads, so cars can keep driving while the new road is built. This describes ways for the old and new Internet to share space.

questions: how to transition from ipv4 to ipv6
what is dual stack and tunneling
how does ipv6 over ipv4 tunneling work
subtitle: Methods for IPv6 hosts and routers to coexist with IPv4

tldr.problem: IPv6 cannot replace IPv4 overnight; the two must coexist for years while infrastructure is built. IPv6 hosts and routers need ways to communicate through IPv4-only networks.
tldr.mechanism: The dual IP layer lets systems run both IPv4 and IPv6. IPv6-over-IPv4 tunneling wraps IPv6 packets in IPv4 headers so they cross IPv4 infrastructure. IPv4-compatible addresses embed an IPv4 address in an IPv6 address for automatic tunneling.
tldr.outcome: IPv6 nodes can operate in a mixed IPv4/IPv6 environment, sending to IPv6 hosts directly and tunneling to others through IPv4. RFC 2893 replaced it with similar mechanisms.

today: RFC 1933 is an Internet Standard. It was superseded by RFC 2893, which made refinements to the transition mechanisms.

sections.title: Why Both Protocols Are Needed
sections.content:
Replacing IPv4 with IPv6 across the entire Internet at once is impossible. IPv4 is deployed in billions of devices and will run for decades. IPv6 must be deployable in a mixed environment, where some nodes understand only IPv4, some understand only IPv6, and many understand both.

This RFC specifies mechanisms for IPv6/IPv4 nodes—systems that implement both protocols—to maintain compatibility with IPv4-only nodes and to use IPv4 routing infrastructure to carry IPv6 traffic. Most Internet nodes will likely need such compatibility for a long time.
sections.eli5: You can't stop building roads and rebuild them all at once. You need the old roads to work while you slowly add the new ones.

sections.title: IPv4-Compatible Addresses
sections.content:
An IPv4-compatible IPv6 address has a special structure: a 96-bit prefix of all zeros followed by a 32-bit IPv4 address. This lets a single address serve both as an IPv6 and an IPv4 address. A node configured with such an address uses the full 128-bit value as its IPv6 address and the last 32 bits as its IPv4 address.

IPv6/IPv4 nodes can acquire IPv4-compatible addresses in two ways: from IPv6 address configuration mechanisms (like stateless auto-configuration or DHCP for IPv6), or by taking an IPv4 address from IPv4 configuration protocols and mapping it by prepending the 96-bit zero prefix. The second approach lets nodes leverage existing IPv4 address servers when IPv6 infrastructure is not yet deployed.
sections.eli5: A special address format lets one number work as both an old-style address and a new-style address.

sections.title: Dual IP Layer Operation
sections.content:
An IPv6/IPv4 node implements both protocols in full. It sends and receives both IPv4 and IPv6 packets, interoperating directly with IPv4-only and IPv6-only nodes using their respective protocols. These nodes may or may not support tunneling.

Nodes can be configured with related or unrelated IPv4 and IPv6 addresses. Those performing automatic tunneling use IPv4-compatible addresses; those doing only configured tunneling set addresses independently. DNS support requires handling both A records (IPv4) and AAAA records (IPv6). When an IPv4-compatible address appears in DNS with both record types, the resolver library can return one or both addresses, affecting whether communication uses IPv4 directly or IPv6 (often tunneled).
sections.eli5: Some computers speak both languages equally well and can understand anyone they meet.

sections.title: IPv6-over-IPv4 Tunneling
sections.content:
A tunnel is a path between two points, allowing packets of one type to cross infrastructure that does not understand them. IPv6 packets are encapsulated inside IPv4 headers, carrying IPv6 traffic across IPv4-only regions. The encapsulating node adds an IPv4 header before the IPv6 packet; the decapsulating node removes it on arrival.

Tunneling takes two forms. In configured tunneling, the tunnel endpoint address is explicitly configured on the sender. The sender tunnels to an intermediary router that will forward the packet onward. In automatic tunneling, the tunnel endpoint address is derived from the destination IPv6 address itself. If that address is IPv4-compatible, the embedded IPv4 address becomes the tunnel destination. This approach works when the packet is tunneled all the way to its final destination.
sections.eli5: You wrap the new-protocol message in an old-protocol envelope to send it through old-protocol networks, then unwrap it at the other end.

sections.title: Tunnel Parameters and Path MTU
sections.content:
When encapsulating IPv6 in IPv4, the encapsulating node must handle fragmentation carefully. Rather than allowing the IPv4 layer to fragment encapsulated packets at routers (which wastes space and reassembly effort), IPv6 should treat the tunnel as a link layer with an MTU equal to the IPv4 path MTU minus 20 bytes for the IPv4 header. The node tracks this MTU using IPv4 Path MTU Discovery.

If the tunnel's MTU would drop below 576 bytes (the IPv6 minimum), IPv4 fragmentation becomes necessary, but the encapsulating node should instead return an IPv6 ICMP "packet too big" error for packets larger than 576 bytes. This strategy minimizes fragmentation while ensuring packets sent are handled correctly by the tunnel. The hop limit is decremented by 1 during tunneling so the tunnel appears as a single hop and remains hidden from diagnostic tools like traceroute.
sections.eli5: Plan for the width of the tunnel and tell the sender what size packages it can send, so nothing gets stuck or mangled.

sections.title: Error Handling and IPv4 ICMP
sections.content: When IPv4 routers inside a tunnel encounter errors (such as "packet too big"), they send IPv4 ICMP error messages back to the encapsulating node. The encapsulating node must translate these into IPv6 ICMP errors for the source. If the ICMP error message includes enough data (the original packet's header and first 8 bytes), the node can extract the original IPv6 header and create a proper IPv6 ICMP error directed to the source node. Older IPv4 routers return only 8 bytes of data, which may not be enough; in such cases the IPv4 ICMP error is handled at the tunnel level and does not propagate backward.
sections.eli5: If something goes wrong inside the tunnel, error messages are unwrapped and sent back in the language the original sender understands.
